blocks.html: Think about the reservation counter at Patna Junction. You fill in a form with your name, age, train number and date. The clerk types these details, the system checks whether a seat is free, and a ticket with a PNR number is printed in a few seconds. That reservation system is doing exactly what every computer does:

items.html: It takes input — your details.
It processes the input — checks seats, calculates the fare, allots a berth.
It gives output — the printed ticket.
It stores — your booking is saved so that the TTE can check it on the train.

blocks.html: Definition: A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data as input, processes it according to a set of instructions (a program), stores it, and produces useful information as output.
The word comes from compute, which means to calculate. Early computers were used only for calculation; today they also play music, show maps, control traffic lights and land spacecraft.

rows: Example: "Riya scored 389 out of 500, which is 77.8%"
Has little meaning on its own

blocks.html: This cycle — Input → Process → Output, with Storage alongside — is called the IPO cycle.

items.html: Speed — A computer can carry out billions of instructions per second. Processor speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz). A result list of lakhs of board students is prepared in minutes.
Accuracy — If the data and the program are correct, the result is always correct. Errors are almost always caused by humans, not by the machine.
Storage — A small pen drive can store thousands of books. Data can be kept for years and found again in seconds.
Diligence — A computer does not get tired or bored. The millionth calculation is done as carefully as the first.
Versatility — The same computer can be used to type a letter, edit a photo, play a game and make a video call.
Automation — Once a program is given, the computer carries out all the steps by itself, without human help at every step.
Reliability — Modern computers work for long hours without failure.
No intelligence of its own (zero IQ): a computer only does what it is told. It cannot decide what should be done.
No feelings: it cannot judge emotions, taste or common sense.
GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out: if wrong data is entered, wrong results come out. If a teacher types 9 instead of 90, the computer will happily show a failing mark.
Dependence on electricity and, for many tasks, on the internet.

blocks.html: Did you know? Artificial Intelligence (AI) lets computers appear to think — for example, a voice assistant that understands Hindi. But even AI works by learning patterns from huge amounts of data that humans provide.
Humans have always looked for tools to count and calculate faster.

items.html: TIFRAC (1960) at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, was the first computer designed and built in India.
C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing), Pune, built PARAM 8000 in 1991 — India's first supercomputer.
Under the National Supercomputing Mission, India now runs many PARAM supercomputers in IITs and research centres, and the AIRAWAT system for AI research.

Laptop, mobile phone, digital watch, calculator

items.html: Supercomputer — the fastest and most expensive. Used for weather forecasting (IMD's monsoon prediction), space research (ISRO), nuclear research and climate studies.
Mainframe — large, powerful machines that handle thousands of users at the same time. Used by banks (SBI's core banking), railways (IRCTC) and insurance companies.
Minicomputer / Server — medium-sized machines that serve a department, a college or a website.
Microcomputer — built around a single microprocessor; meant for one user.
Desktop, laptop (notebook), tablet, smartphone, smartwatch
Embedded computer — a small computer built inside another device to do one job: washing machine, microwave, car engine control, ATM, smart TV.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.1 · Block diagram of a computer

blocks.html: A computer system has four main parts:

items.html: Input unit — accepts data and instructions from the user and converts them into a form (binary) the computer understands. Examples: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone.
Central Processing Unit (CPU) — the brain of the computer. It has three parts:
Control Unit (CU): fetches each instruction, decodes it and directs the other units — like a traffic policeman at a crossing.
Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): does arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical comparisons (>, <, =, AND, OR).
Registers: very small, very fast storage places inside the CPU that hold the data being worked on at that instant.
Memory (storage) unit — holds data, programs and results. Primary memory (RAM) holds what is in use now; secondary storage (hard disk, SSD) keeps it permanently. (Chapter 2 covers these in detail.)
Output unit — converts the results from binary into a form humans understand. Examples: monitor, printer, speaker.

blocks.html: Worked example — adding two marks: You type 45 and 38 (input). The CU fetches the "add" instruction, the ALU adds the two numbers, the result 83 is placed in a register and then in memory, and finally it appears on the screen (output).

items.html: Hardware — the physical parts you can touch: monitor, keyboard, CPU chip, cables, printer.
Software — the set of programs that tells the hardware what to do. You cannot touch it.
Humanware (liveware) — the people who use, operate and build computer systems.
Firmware — software permanently stored in a ROM chip, such as the BIOS that starts the computer.

blocks.html: Hardware without software is like a body without life; software without hardware is like a song with no singer.

rows: Runs and manages the computer itself
Operating systems (Windows, Linux, Android), device drivers
Helps the user do a specific job
MS Word, Excel, Tally, Paint, web browsers, games, BHIM UPI

lessons.title: 1.7 How a computer stores data: bits and bytes

blocks.html: A computer is made of millions of tiny switches that can be either ON (1) or OFF (0). So everything — numbers, letters, photos, songs — is stored as patterns of 0s and 1s. This is the binary number system (base 2).
Convert 13 to binary: divide by 2 repeatedly and write the remainders.
Read the remainders from bottom to top: 13 = 1101 in binary.
Place values in binary are powers of 2: … 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

Did you know? The letter 'A' is stored as the number 65 (binary 01000001) using a code called ASCII. Hindi and other Indian scripts are stored using Unicode, which can represent characters from almost every language in the world.
Aim: To identify the parts of a computer and follow the IPO cycle.
You need: a desktop computer in the lab, a notebook.

items.html: Identify the parts. With your teacher's help, list every device connected to the computer. Write each under one heading: Input, Output, Storage or Processing.
Look at the back of the cabinet. Find the ports for power, monitor (VGA/HDMI), USB and network (LAN). Draw them in your notebook.
Start the computer. Note what appears on the screen while it starts (maker's logo, then Windows). This start-up process is called booting.
Check the system details. Press Windows key + Pause/Break, or open Settings → System → About. Write down the processor name and speed, the installed RAM and the Windows edition.
Trace the IPO cycle. Open the Calculator, type 245 × 16 and press Enter. In your notebook, write which part did the input, which did the processing and which showed the output.
Binary challenge. In Calculator, choose Programmer mode. Type 25 in DEC and read the BIN value. Then check your own working by the division method (answer: 11001).

items.html: A computer accepts data, processes it under the control of a program, stores it and gives information as output (IPO cycle).
Its strengths are speed, accuracy, storage, diligence, versatility and automation; its limitations are no intelligence, no feelings and GIGO.
Charles Babbage is the Father of the Computer; Ada Lovelace was the first programmer; ENIAC was the first general-purpose electronic computer.
The five generations were based on vacuum tubes, transistors, ICs, microprocessors and AI.
Computers are analog, digital or hybrid by working, and super, mainframe, mini, micro or embedded by size.
The CPU has a Control Unit, an ALU and registers; it works with input, output and memory units.
Hardware is physical; software is the set of programs; firmware is software stored in ROM.
Computers store everything in binary; 8 bits make a byte and 1024 bytes make a kilobyte.
